newsitem.title: USA: Former Towers executives indicted for conspiracy.
newsitem.headline: Former Towers executives indicted for conspiracy.

text.p: Two former high ranking officers of Towers Financial Corp., Steven Hoffenberg's scandal-ridden bill collection business, have been indicted for conspiracy and securities fraud, prosecutors said Thursday.

Mitchell Brater, 54, of South Salem, N.Y., former vice chairman of the board of directors, and Michael Rosoff, 47, of Chappaqua, N.Y., Towers' former general counsel, were named in a six-count indictment filed in Manhattan federal court.

In addition to the conspiracy and securities fraud charges, they are accused of obstruction of justice and perjury in connection with Towers' fraudulent sale of more than $270 million in promissory notes between 1986 and 1993.
If convicted Brater faces a possible sentence of 35 years in prison and Rosoff faces 45 years. They both face possible fines of $3.25 million.
The Securities and Exchange Commission previously filed related civil suits against Brater and Rosoff. Those suits are still pending.
Towers filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 1993 after it was found that former owner Hoffenberg used the company to operate what prosecutors say is the largest Ponzi scheme in history.

Hoffenberg, who gained national attention when he offered to rescue the New York Post in January 1993, pleaded guilty to conspiracy and fraud charges in April 1995. He was sentenced last month to 20 years in prison and ordered to pay more than $462 million in restitution to the more than 3,000 investors who bought Towers notes and securities.
He was charged with selling fraudulent notes and bonds to investors and used some of the money he collected from later investors to pay interest owed to the earlier ones.

The rest of the money was used to run the Post for a few weeks and to operate his financial empire with inflated revenues and bogus profits that made it appear to be a major health care financing company.
